title: Identity and System — whoami, id, uname
lead: Before you touch a system, answer two questions: Who am I? Which machine am I on? This module teaches you how, using safe read-only commands.
objectives: You read your user identity, UID/GID values and group memberships with `whoami`, `id` and `groups`.
You find the machine name, kernel version and architecture with `hostname` and `uname`.
You identify the distribution and its version with `/etc/os-release`.
You see the time and how long the system has been running with `date` and `uptime`.
You read disk and memory usage with `df -h` and `free -h`.
You use environment variables with `env` and `$USER`.

sections.title: Who am I? whoami, id, groups
body: Before you run a command you should know which account you are using: a normal user or an administrator? A command run with the wrong account either fails or does more damage than intended because of excess privileges.

`whoami` prints only the user name. `id` says more: the numeric user ID **UID**, the primary group ID **GID** and all groups you belong to. Linux permissions look at these numbers, not at names. UID 0 is always **root** (the administrator); normal users usually start at 1000.

`groups` lists the same groups, names only. In this course the user `student` belongs to the groups `student`, `wheel` and `devs`. `wheel` is the administrator group that allows `sudo` on the RHEL family (on Ubuntu this group is called `sudo`).

commands.what: Prints the current user name.
commands.where: After logging in, after using `sudo`, or inside a script.
commands.why: Prevents actions with the wrong user.

commands.what: Shows UID, GID and all groups.
commands.where: When investigating `Permission denied` errors.
commands.why: Permissions are checked by numbers and group membership.

commands.what: Lists the names of the groups you belong to.
commands.where: To check whether you can reach a file through a group.
commands.why: Shorter and easier to read than `id`.

commands.what: Prints only the UID number.
commands.where: In scripts, to test whether you are root (0 = root).
commands.why: A single number is easy to compare in a script.

sections.tip: `whoami` gives a name, `id` gives the numbers the system really uses. When in doubt, run `id`.

sections.title: Which machine? hostname and uname
body: When you have several servers or VMs, their command lines all look alike. `hostname` tells you the machine's name on the network; it is the cheapest way to confirm you are on the right machine before a destructive command.

`uname` reports on the kernel. `uname -r` prints the kernel release, `uname -m` the architecture (`x86_64` = 64-bit Intel/AMD, `aarch64` = ARM) and `uname -a` everything in one line. You are asked for these values when opening a support ticket or downloading software.

commands.what: Prints the machine's name.
commands.where: To tell servers apart, when writing a ticket.
commands.why: Prevents working on the wrong machine.

commands.what: Prints the running kernel version.
commands.where: For bug reports or driver compatibility checks.
commands.why: The kernel version decides which features exist.

commands.what: Prints the machine architecture.
commands.where: Before downloading a package or ISO.
commands.why: Packages are built per architecture.

commands.what: Prints all system information on one line.
commands.where: To paste into a support request.
commands.why: Name, kernel and architecture at once.

commands.what: Prints the machine's IP address(es).
commands.where: When you want to connect to your VM via SSH.
commands.why: The shortest way to find the address.

sections.tip: The `student@linux-lab` part of the prompt is user@machine; `whoami` and `hostname` give the same information.

sections.title: Which distribution? /etc/os-release
body: Even with the same kernel, distributions differ. The distribution name and version are stored as plain text in `/etc/os-release`, in the same format on Ubuntu, Rocky, Alma and others. You read it with `cat`; you do not change it.
`NAME` and `VERSION` give the readable name, `PRETTY_NAME` a one-line summary, and `ID_LIKE` the family (`debian` or `rhel fedora`). The family tells you which package manager to use: `apt` or `dnf`.

commands.what: Shows the complete distribution information.
commands.where: As the first step on a new system.
commands.why: Decides which commands and packages apply.

commands.what: Shows only the readable distribution name.
commands.where: To put a single line into a ticket.
commands.why: Filters the one line you need out of a longer file.

commands.what: Shows the family the distribution belongs to.
commands.where: When you are unsure whether to use `apt` or `dnf`.
commands.why: The family determines the package manager.

sections.tip: WSL has the same file; it shows the Linux distribution inside, not Windows.

sections.title: Time and uptime: date, uptime
body: `date` prints the system time and time zone. You need it when reading logs and when putting dates in backup file names. You can change the format with a pattern starting with `+`: `date +%F` → `2026-11-12`.

`uptime` gives three things on one line: the time, how long the system has been running and the **load average** for the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes. If the load is far above the number of CPU cores, the system is slow. You also notice unexpected reboots here.

commands.what: Prints the current date and time.
commands.where: When matching log entries to times.
commands.why: A wrong clock is a common cause of certificate and log problems.

commands.what: Prints the date as YYYY-MM-DD.
commands.where: When adding a date to file names (`backup-2026-11-12`).
commands.why: A consistent format that sorts alphabetically.

commands.what: Shows uptime and load average.
commands.where: The first place to look when the system is slow.
commands.why: Quickly shows load and the last reboot.

commands.what: Prints uptime in readable form (`up 2 days, 3 hours`).
commands.where: To report the duration briefly.
commands.why: Gives only the duration, without load figures.

sections.tip: Compare the load average with the core count: on 4 cores, 4.0 means fully busy.

sections.title: Disk and memory: df -h, free -h
body: `df` (disk free) shows how full the mounted file systems are. `-h` (human-readable) uses units like `G` and `M` instead of bytes. If the `Use%` column goes above 90%, take care: a full disk makes services crash.

`free` shows memory (RAM) and swap. The important column is `available`: the memory that can be given to new programs. A small `free` value is normal, because Linux uses spare memory as cache (`buff/cache`).
Both only read; neither changes anything.

commands.what: Shows size and usage of all file systems.
commands.where: On a `No space left on device` error.
commands.why: Finds out which partition is full.

commands.what: Shows only the root file system.
commands.where: When checking a single partition.
commands.why: Keeps the output short.

commands.what: Shows memory and swap usage in readable units.
commands.where: When the system is slow.
commands.why: The `available` column shows the memory that is really free.

sections.warn: `df` measures file systems, `du` measures folders; do not mix them up. You find a full disk with `df -h` and look for the cause with tools you will meet in later modules.
sections.tip: Do not worry about a small value in the `free` column of `free` output; look at `available`.

sections.title: Environment variables: env and $USER
body: The shell stores information in **environment variables**. `$USER` holds the user name, `$HOME` the home directory, `$SHELL` the shell and `$HOSTNAME` the machine name. You use a value by putting `$` in front: `echo $USER`.
`env` lists all variables as `NAME=value`. To pick a single one from the long output, combine it with `grep` using `|` (pipe): `env | grep USER`.
Variables are handy in scripts: `echo "$USER@$(hostname)"` combines the user and the machine. The output of the command inside `$(...)` is inserted in its place.

commands.what: Lists all environment variables.
commands.where: When investigating where a setting comes from.
commands.why: Shows the values you are running with.

commands.what: Prints the value of the user name variable.
commands.where: In scripts and file names.
commands.why: You do not have to type the user name by hand.

commands.what: Prints the path of the home directory.
commands.where: To write portable paths.
commands.why: Works for every user instead of a fixed `/home/student`.

commands.what: Filters the variables whose name contains USER.
commands.where: To find one variable in a long list.
commands.why: A pipe and `grep` narrow down the output.

commands.what: Combines user and machine name.
commands.where: When building a report line or log message.
commands.why: Shows how a variable and command output are combined.

commands.what: Prints the value of a single variable.
commands.where: In a script when you need only the value.
commands.why: No `grep` needed, the output is just the value.

sections.tip: Variable names are case-sensitive: `$USER` works, `$user` is empty.

t01.text: Find out which user you are with `whoami`.

t02.text: Find out the machine's name with `hostname`.
t02.hint: It should match the part after `@` in the prompt.

t04.text: Run `id` to see UID, GID and all groups.
t04.hint: If `uid=` is 1000 you are a normal user, if 0 you are root.

t05.text: List your groups with `groups` and compare with the `id` output.

t07.text: See how long the system has been running and the load average with `uptime`.
t07.hint: The last three numbers are the 1, 5 and 15 minute load.

t08.text: Run `df -h` to see disk usage in readable units.

t09.hint: The really free memory is in the `available` column.

t10.text: Among the environment variables, filter only those containing USER: `env | grep USER`.
t10.hint: The `|` sign passes the output of `env` to `grep`.

t11.text: Predict: is the user `student` in the group `devs`? Then verify with `groups`.
t11.hint: Say your guess first, then run the command.

t12.text: Predict: what does `echo "$USER@$(hostname)"` print? Verify by running it.
t12.hint: `$USER` and `$(hostname)` are replaced by their values before the command runs.

t13.text: The file `~/kernel.txt` contains an old kernel version. Fix it so it holds the real kernel version.
t13.hint: `uname -r > ~/kernel.txt` overwrites the old content. Then check with `cat ~/kernel.txt`.

t14.text: Create `~/me.txt` containing, in order, the output of `whoami`, `id` and `hostname` (3 lines).
t14.hint: Use `>` for the first and `>>` for the others: `whoami > ~/me.txt`, `id >> ~/me.txt`.

t15.text: Write the readable distribution name, without the `PRETTY_NAME=` prefix, into `~/distro.txt`.
t15.hint: `grep PRETTY_NAME /etc/os-release | cut -d= -f2 > ~/distro.txt`: `cut` takes what follows the `=` sign.

t16.text: Write only the major number (first number) of the kernel version into `~/major.txt`.
t16.hint: Take the output of `uname -r`, split it at the dot with `cut -d. -f1` and keep the first field.

t17.text: Ticket: Support wants system information. Write the machine name, kernel version, user name and the `df -h` output, in that order, into `~/sysinfo.txt`.
t17.hint: Start with `hostname > ~/sysinfo.txt`, then append the other four outputs with `>>`.

t18.text: Ticket: The administrator asks whether the account `student` is in the `wheel` group. As evidence, save only the output containing `wheel` into `~/admin_check.txt`.

vm.intro: All commands in this section are read-only; you can run them safely on your VM. Output may differ by distribution; what matters is that you recognise the structure.

v01.title: Find your identity
v01.text: Show your user name, UID/GID values and groups; paste the `id` output.

blocks.expected:
student
uid=1000(student) gid=1000(student) groups=1000(student),10(wheel)
student wheel

differs: On Ubuntu the administrator group is called `sudo`, not `wheel`; in the `id` output you see `27(sudo)`.
Your user name may not be `student`; that is fine, just see your own name.

v02.title: Machine and kernel
v02.text: Show the machine name and the full kernel information; paste the `uname -a` output.

blocks.expected:
linux-lab
5.14.0-427.el9.x86_64
x86_64
Linux linux-lab 5.14.0-427.el9.x86_64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC ... x86_64 GNU/Linux

differs: Your kernel version may differ (`6.8...` on Ubuntu 24.04); what matters is that the output starts with `Linux`.
On a VM on Apple Silicon the architecture shows `aarch64`.

v03.title: Know your distribution
v03.text: Read the distribution information and paste the output.

blocks.expected:
NAME="Rocky Linux"
VERSION="9.4 (Blue Onyx)"
PRETTY_NAME="Rocky Linux 9.4 (Blue Onyx)"
ID_LIKE="rhel centos fedora"

differs: On Ubuntu you see `ID_LIKE=debian`; on Rocky/Alma it contains `rhel`.
Some distributions have no `ID_LIKE` line at all (for example Debian itself); `grep` then prints nothing.

v04.title: Time and uptime
v04.text: Show the date and how long the system has been running; paste the `uptime` output.
differs: On a freshly started VM the uptime is shown in minutes (`up 12 min`).
The date format and time zone can vary with the system language.

v05.title: Disk and memory
v05.text: Show disk and memory status in readable units; paste both outputs together.

blocks.expected:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/mapper/rhel-root  20G  4.1G  16G  21% /
...
               total        used        free  ...
Mem:           3.8Gi       612Mi       2.4Gi ...

differs: On WSL the `df -h` output also lists the Windows drives (`C:\`).
The memory columns show different numbers depending on your VM settings.

v06.title: Environment variables
v06.text: Print the user variable and filter it from the `env` output.

blocks.cmd:
echo $USER
echo $HOME
env | grep USER
echo "$USER@$(hostname)"

differs: `env | grep USER` may return several lines (for example ones matching `XDG_SESSION_...`); look for the `USER=` line.
On some systems `$USER` is empty (for example inside a container); `whoami` still works.

v07.title: See the administrator identity
v07.text: Run `whoami` with `sudo`: the command now runs as root. If it asks for a password, type your account's password (it is not shown while typing).
differs: If you get `student is not in the sudoers file`, your account is not in the administrator group; try the user you created during installation.
`root` must appear in the middle; `sudo` elevates only that one command, afterwards you are a normal user again.

q1.q: You see `uid=0(...)` in the `id` output. What does it mean?
options: The user belongs to no group
q1.explain: UID 0 always belongs to root. Normal users usually get a UID of 1000 or higher.

q2.q: Which command shows the running kernel version?
q2.explain: `uname -r` prints the kernel version. `hostname` shows the machine name, `whoami` the user, `df -h` the disk.

q3.q: Which command shows disk usage in readable units (GB, MB)?
q3.explain: `df -h` shows file systems. `free -h` shows memory, `uptime` the running time.

q4.q: Which environment variable holds the current user's name?
q4.explain: `$USER` holds the user name; `$HOME` holds the home directory, `$SHELL` the shell.

summary: `whoami`, `id`, `groups`: show who you are and which permissions you have; UID 0 = root.
`hostname` and `uname -r/-m/-a`: machine name, kernel version and architecture.
`date` and `uptime`: the time, and the uptime with the load average.
`df -h` and `free -h`: disk and memory status; for memory look at the `available` column.
`env`, `$USER`, `$HOME`: environment variables; you use a value with `$`.
Before starting any task, check who you are and which machine you are on.

glossary.meaning: User number; permission checks use this number, not names. 0 = root.
Group number; identifies the user's primary group.
The administrator group that grants `sudo` on the RHEL family (`sudo` on Ubuntu).
The Linux core that manages the hardware; its version is shown by `uname -r`.
The machine's name on the network.
Average system load over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes; shown by `uptime`.
A `NAME=value` pair kept by the shell, for example `USER` or `HOME`.
